title: The Citizens Rejoice in the Arena
story:
The wrestling festival of King Kamsa had been meant to end in one thing: the death of Krishna and his brother Balarama, the two cowherd boys from Vrindavan whom the king had feared for years, ever since a prophecy said that Krishna would end his reign. But the trap had failed at its very first teeth — the great elephant set at the arena gate lay dead, killed by Krishna — and now the brothers walked into the arena, Krishna carrying one of the tusks in his hand. The city looked down at the two of them and forgot, for a moment, that it had come to watch them die.

They shone as they entered — great-armed, in bright garments, garlands and ornaments, the tusk carried like a staff of proof — and the crowd's eyes followed them across the sand. The galleries were full: townsmen and countrymen, kings and commoners, wrestlers and merchants, women at the screened windows, all standing on the tiers and leaning forward over the rail. They drank the sight of the two young men in, unable to look away from what stood below them.

Then the people began to speak of them to one another, and what each one said was the same and yet different, for everyone saw the two according to his own heart. To the wrestlers they whispered that this one was a thunderbolt. To ordinary men he was the best of men. To the women he was love itself given a form. To the cowherds of Vrindavan he was one of their own, come in from the pastures. To the wicked among the kings he was a chastiser, come to call them to account. To the ignorant he was the highest truth; to the yogis, the end of all their striving; to his own kinsmen, the Vrishnis, he was their supreme deity. To his parents he was still only a child. And to Kamsa, seated high above them, he was death walking in through the gate.

And as they looked, the people began to remember aloud what they had heard of this boy. They told how he was born to Devaki and carried away in the night to Gokula. How the demoness Putana had come to him as a nurse and been brought to an end, and the whirlwind demon that had snatched him up after her. How he had saved the cows and the cowherds from the forest fire, and how he had held up a great hill on one hand for seven whole days. They spoke of the gopis, the cowgirls of Vrindavan, who never tired of his smiling, glancing face, and of how he had made the line of Yadu — the royal family he was born into — famous in every land. And this one beside him, they said, is his elder brother — the glorious Balarama, with the lotus eyes.

The trumpets were still sounding, but above them rose another sound: the murmur of a crowd realizing, all at once, who it was that had walked into its arena. The two they had come to see as victims were being named, from every side and in every way, as something far older and far larger than the sport of an afternoon. The rejoicing filled the galleries before a single blow of the wrestling had been struck.
reflection: The crowd does not settle on one description as the true one. Krishna is all of them at once — thunderbolt and kinsman, child and death — and each person, for a moment, sees him as his or her own heart is ready for. Recognition is the whole event, and it happens before the fight.
next_story_tease: But the rejoicing did not last; Chanura was already stepping forward.
hero_scene: Krishna and Balarama entering the Mathura arena, Krishna still carrying the elephant's tusk, while the crowded galleries lean forward, every face turned down toward the two brothers, wonder and joy rising like a tide.
